title: Toward a standardized evaluation of imputation methodology
text:
Presenter: Hanne Oberman, Utrecht University
Co-authors: Gerko Vink (Utrecht University)

Abstract
Simulation studies have become a flexible and easy tool for evaluating new methodology. Unfortunately, there is no consensus on how to perform simulation studies for the evaluation of missing data methodology, such as imputation. We suggest a course of action for simulating and evaluating missing data problems. Our suggested course of action is by no means meant to serve as a complete cookbook, but rather meant to incite critical thinking and a move to objective and fair evaluations of imputation methodology. We invite the audience to take part in the discussion, contribute to our proposed simulation checklist, and imagine how this may relate to preregistration templates for simulation studies.

The aim of this event is to bring together researchers from different fields of methodological research (including, but not limited to (bio)statistics, psychometrics, econometrics, bioinformatics, machine learning, quantitative methods for ecology, linguistics, etc.) who are interested in meta science on methods research, discuss how new quantitative methods are developed, evaluated and published in our respective fields, and how this process can be improved by sharing our thoughts and experiences across disciplines.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
Code of Conduct
We are dedicated to providing a supportive, collegial, and harassment-free conference experience for everyone, regardless of: gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, age, or religion, intellectual position, approaches to data analysis, software preferences, coding style, scientific perspective, etc.
The Code of Conduct applies to this event, including but not limited to the talks, poster sessions, and social activities. We do not tolerate harassment, intimidation, or bullying of conference participants. Sexual language and imagery are not appropriate in presentations, communications, in online venues, including chats.
Conference participants violating these rules may be sanctioned or expelled from the conference at the discretion of the conference organizers.

Examples of unacceptable harassment, intimidation, and bullying behavior
Harassment includes, but is not limited to: Making comments in chats, to an audience or personally, that belittle or demean another person; harassing photography or recording; sustained disruption of talks or other events; unwelcome sexual attention; advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior.
Intimidation and bullying include, but are not limited to: aggressive or browbeating behavior directed at someone during a public presentation; mocking or insulting another person’s intellect, work, perspective, or question/comment; making reference to someone’s gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, age, religion, or other personal attributes in the context of a scientific discussion; deliberately making someone feel unwelcome.


Enforcement
Participants asked to stop any harassing behavior are expected to comply immediately. If a participant engages in harassing behavior, event organizers retain the right to take any actions to keep the event a welcoming environment for all participants. This includes warning the offender or expulsion from the conference.
We expect participants to follow these rules at all event venues and event-related online activities.


Reporting
If someone makes you or anyone else feel unsafe or unwelcome, please report it as soon as possible to members of the local organizing committee (Anne-Laure Boulesteix, Moritz Herrmann, Marieke Stolte, Edouard Bonneville). Harassment and other code of conduct violations reduce the value of our event for everyone. We want you to be happy at our event. People like you make our event a better place.
When taking a personal report, our staff will ensure you are safe and cannot be overheard. They may involve other event staff to ensure your report is managed properly. Once safe, we’ll ask you to tell us about what happened. This can be upsetting, but we’ll handle it as respectfully as possible, and you can bring someone to support you. You won’t be asked to confront anyone, and we won’t tell anyone who you are.
Our team will be happy to help you contact hotel/venue security, local law enforcement, local support services, provide escorts, or otherwise assist you to feel safe for the duration of the event. We value your attendance.


Source
This code of conduct was adapted from the Bioconductor project and the Modern Benchmarking conference.

title: Trust and trustworthiness of research on biostatistical methods
text:
Speaker: Tim Morris, Novartis

Abstract
With the best of intentions and sharpest of focus, it can be difficult to fully understand a contribution to methodological research. We are often left wondering, `Is it me, or is there a problem with the work?’ Ultimately, we are then left to decide whether or not to take the conclusions on trust. Repeatedly observing that a new method is better than all existing methods may undermine our trust. The same problem has faced many empirical sciences and led to the introduction of structures, with varying degrees of success. In this talk, I will discuss some structures and ideas that may improve the trustworthiness of biostatistical methodology research, arguing against imposing too many – if any – as hard rules.

title: Call for Contributions
text:
Call for Contributions
Across many scientific disciplines, observed reproducibility issues have led to increased meta-scientific research and the adoption of open science policies, reshaping how empirical research is conducted and evaluated. Methodological research disciplines — disciplines that develop and evaluate the methods underlying empirical research such as (bio)statistics, psychometrics, econometrics, bioinformatics, machine learning, and quantitative methods for ecology, linguistics, etc. — have so far received little meta-scientific attention, and have yet to embrace similar reforms. Yet, there is also evidence of problematic practices and reproducibility issues in methodological research, such as selective or incomplete reporting, selective manipulation of simulation parameters, unequal treatment due to asymmetric familiarity with compared methods, improper handling of method failures, etc.
But things are beginning to change. Across a number of methodological disciplines, researchers have started to investigate how methods are developed, evaluated and published in their own fields, what problems occur in this process and how it could be improved. At the moment, these efforts remain largely isolated within specific disciplines, with little cross-disciplinary exchange and no shared vocabulary for thinking and talking about scientific rigor in methods research in general. The 2st Interdisciplinary Symposium on Meta Science for Methods Research aims to bridge this gap by bringing different methodological communities together for the first time to share insights and experiences, build a common ground, and collectively advance meta science for methods research.
The event will focus not on the methodological innovations themselves, like our typical conferences, but rather how we as a scientific community organize ourselves to digest the explosion of “novel” computational and statistical methods, what measures we can take ourselves in our roles as scientists, supervisors and reviewers to make methods research more trustworthy, but also what needs to change in institutions or the publication system to shift incentives away from problematic practices.
Topics of interest include, but are not limited to (and are not mutually exclusive):

Conceptual work: Defining and discussing what concepts such as replicability or generalizability mean for methodological research and how or to what extent recommendations on good scientific practice from other disciplines transfer to methods research
Tools and practices: Concrete tools or suggestions (for example, software, platforms, templates, checklists) for improving methods research workflows
Empirical meta scientific work: Literature reviews on reporting practices, self-report surveys among methods researchers, many-analysts simulation studies, etc., shedding light into how methodological research is currently done, possibly leading to suggestions for improvement
Policy proposals: Suggestions how changes, for example, in our supervision, tenure or publication system could shift incentives away from problematic practices
